The n-ball and the Gamma function

Volume and surface area of the unit ball in every real dimension n, and |Γ| on the real line with its poles. One function, from the circle upward. A picture shows a structure; it is not evidence that the structure means anything beyond its definition.

Volume V and sphere area S of the unit ball.
V = π^(n/2)/Γ(n/2+1)S = 2π^(n/2)/Γ(n/2) = n·V
Hover the plot.
Any real n.
|Γ(x)| on the real line. poles at 0, −1, −2, … (red lines); Γ(x) = ∫₀^∞ t^(x−1) e^(−t) dt for x > 0, continued by Γ(x) = Γ(x+1)/x.
Hover.
About this visual

What you are looking at. Two curves of one function. Top: the volume V and the surface area S of the unit ball in n dimensions, drawn for every real n, not only whole numbers. The Gamma function is what makes that possible: V = π^(n/2) / Γ(n/2 + 1) and S = 2π^(n/2) / Γ(n/2) = n·V. Bottom: |Γ(x)| on the real line, with its poles at 0, −1, −2, … marked in red.

How to read it. Marks on the top plot: the dimensions of the Cayley–Dickson tower (1, 2, 4, 8, 16) and the peaks. Hover for values. The slider gives V, S and Γ(n/2) at any n. At n = 2 the ball is the disc (V = π) and the sphere is the circle (S = 2π, with Γ(1) = 1): the circle is where the whole family starts to be recognisable.

What it shows. V peaks at n = 5.2569 (value 5.2778) and S at n = 7.2569 (value 33.16); after that both fall towards zero, so a 16-dimensional unit ball has volume 0.2353, less than the 2-disc. 5.257 is the 'n* = 5.257' of the RiemannHypothesisProof to-do list. The identity behind Γ: the Gaussian integral of e^(−|x|²) over n dimensions is (√π)^n, and in spherical coordinates it equals (S/2)·Γ(n/2).

What it does not show. That Γ 'is' a hypersphere in a stronger sense than this identity, or that 5.257 matches anything in the sedenion tower: the match to the to-do list's number is noted and not derived. The poles are the places the integral ∫ t^(z−1) e^(−t) dt stops converging, and the function is continued past them; they carry real information (residues (−1)^k / k!) and are not noise.

Numbers to check. Peak V at n = 5.256946, V = 5.277768; peak S at n = 7.256946, S = 33.1612. V(1) = 2, V(2) = π, V(3) = 4π/3, V(8) = 4.0587, V(16) = 0.23533. Γ(1/2) = √π = 1.77245. The browser's Gamma agrees with Python's to 10 significant figures at 8 test points.

Literature.

  • C. F. Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), §VII; P. L. Wantzel, "Recherches sur les moyens de reconnaître si un Problème de Géométrie peut se résoudre avec la règle et le compas", J. Math. Pures Appl. 2 (1837) 366–372. Constructibility of the regular n-gon.
  • H.-V. Niemeier, "Definite quadratische Formen der Dimension 24 und Diskriminante 1", J. Number Theory 5 (1973) 142–178.
  • J. H. Conway and N. J. A. Sloane, Sphere Packings, Lattices and Groups (Springer, 1999), ch. 16 and 18: the 24 Niemeier lattices and their Coxeter numbers; ch. 1: the volume of the n-ball.
  • A. P. Ogg, "Automorphismes de courbes modulaires", Séminaire Delange–Pisot–Poitou 16 (1974/75), exposé 7. The 15 primes dividing the order of the Monster.
  • A. N. Schellekens, "Meromorphic c = 24 conformal field theories", Commun. Math. Phys. 153 (1993) 159–185. The 71 holomorphic c = 24 theories.
  • P. J. Davis, "Leonhard Euler's Integral: A Historical Profile of the Gamma Function", Amer. Math. Monthly 66 (1959) 849–869.
  • G. Veneziano, "Construction of a crossing-symmetric, Regge-behaved amplitude for linearly rising trajectories", Nuovo Cimento A 57 (1968) 190–197. The amplitude was Euler's beta function, Γ(a)Γ(b)/Γ(a+b).
  • H. Darmon and A. Granville, "On the equations z^m = F(x, y) and Ax^p + By^q = Cz^r", Bull. London Math. Soc. 27 (1995) 513–543; F. Beukers, "The Diophantine equation Ax^p + By^q = Cz^r", Duke Math. J. 91 (1998) 61–88. Where generalized Fermat meets the ADE (spherical) signatures.
  • The Python Software Foundation, Python 3 documentation: math.lgamma, math.gamma.
  • OpenSCAD User Manual (camera, projection, multmatrix).
  • MDN Web Docs, Canvas API.
